<browser_instruction># Claude in Chrome browser automation

You have access to browser automation tools (mcp__claude-in-chrome__*) for interacting with web pages in Chrome. Follow these guidelines for effective browser automation.

## Loading deferred tools

If the mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load every tool you expect to need in ONE ToolSearch call — the select query accepts a comma-separated list — never one call per tool. Start with the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting.

## GIF recording

When performing multi-step browser interactions that the user may want to review or share, use mcp__claude-in-chrome__gif_creator to record them.

You must ALWAYS:
* Capture extra frames before and after taking actions to ensure smooth playback
* Name the file meaningfully to help the user identify it later (e.g., "login_process.gif")

## Console log debugging

You can use mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_console_messages to read console output. Console output may be verbose. If you are looking for specific log entries, use the 'pattern' parameter with a regex-compatible pattern. This filters results efficiently and avoids overwhelming output. For example, use pattern: "[MyApp]" to filter for application-specific logs rather than reading all console output.

## Alerts and dialogs

IMPORTANT: Do not trigger JavaScript alerts, confirms, prompts, or browser modal dialogs through your actions. These browser dialogs block all further browser events and will prevent the extension from receiving any subsequent commands. Instead, when possible, use console.log for debugging and then use the mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_console_messages tool to read those log messages. If a page has dialog-triggering elements:
1. Avoid clicking buttons or links that may trigger alerts (e.g., "Delete" buttons with confirmation dialogs)
2. If you must interact with such elements, warn the user first that this may interrupt the session
3. Use mcp__claude-in-chrome__javascript_tool to check for and dismiss any existing dialogs before proceeding

If you accidentally trigger a dialog and lose responsiveness, inform the user they need to manually dismiss it in the browser.

## Avoid rabbit holes and loops

When using browser automation tools, stay focused on the specific task. If you encounter any of the following, stop and ask the user for guidance:
- Unexpected complexity or tangential browser exploration
- Browser tool calls failing or returning errors after 2-3 attempts
- No response from the browser extension
- Page elements not responding to clicks or input
- Pages not loading or timing out
- Unable to complete the browser task despite multiple approaches

Explain what you attempted, what went wrong, and ask how the user would like to proceed. Do not keep retrying the same failing browser action or explore unrelated pages without checking in first.

## Tab context and session startup

IMPORTANT: At the start of each browser automation session, call mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp first to get information about the user's current browser tabs. Use this context to understand what the user might want to work with before creating new tabs.

Never reuse tab IDs from a previous/other session. Follow these guidelines:
1. Only reuse an existing tab if the user explicitly asks to work with it
2. Otherwise, create a new tab with mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp
3. If a tool returns an error indicating the tab doesn't exist or is invalid, call tabs_context_mcp to get fresh tab IDs
4. When a tab is closed by the user or a navigation error occurs, call tabs_context_mcp to see what tabs are available</browser_instruction>

.claude/settings.json | 113 +++++++++++++++++++++++++++-----------------------
 CLAUDE.md             |   5 +++
 2 files changed, 66 insertions(+), 52 deletions(-)
9:1. **One functionality per commit** (where possible). Each commit must be independently reviewable; do not bundle two unrelated changes.
14:2. **Manually test each committed change before starting the next functionality**, in addition to automated coverage. "Tested" means: the affected code path was exercised locally, not just that it compiled.
15:3. **Defects → GitHub issue first, never silent fixes.** Use `gh issue create --title "fix: <desc>"`. The PR that fixes it must include `Fixes #N` in the title or body. This also covers findings deferred out of a `/code-review` pass (rule 1c).
24:4. **Every new functionality ships with unit tests.** Tests live next to the code they cover (`backend/tests/`, `frontend/tests/`).
40:   **4b. Automated accessibility floor — axe-core, ratcheted, not big-bang** ([#1670](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1670), Theme-3 item 1): `serious`/`critical` axe-core violations are checked on every PR, in the existing jobs — no new required check. The Playwright lane (`frontend/e2e/a11y.spec.ts` + `frontend/e2e-otp/a11y.spec.ts` for the sign-in screen, `@axe-core/playwright`) scans **every route, once per theme** against the real seeded stack (dark surfaces are keyed `route:/…@dark`; the sign-in card is white in both themes, so it is scanned once) — a route added to `App.tsx` or `pages/admin/routes.tsx` is added to the spec in the same PR (enforced: `frontend/tests/a11y/scanCoverage.test.ts` parses the routers and fails on a declared path with no scan, and `tests/utils/pageTitle.test.ts` does the same for its document title), and each scan first waits for the page to finish loading (`frontend/scripts/a11y/settle.ts`), because a scan that lands mid-load sees fewer violations and the ratchet cannot tell; the Vitest lane (`frontend/tests/a11y/components.a11y.test.tsx`, `axe-core` run directly against jsdom — **not** the `vitest-axe` npm package, a single-maintainer fork last published over a year ago and never promoted past `0.1.0`, which fails the rule-40 supply-chain bar) covers the check editor, connection form, suite form, results table, and notification panel. Token values axe cannot see — SVG fills, `Progress` strokes, inline-coloured text it silently skips — are held to the WCAG ratios directly by `frontend/tests/a11y/tokens.test.ts`. Keyboard-only operation is its own real-browser spec, `frontend/e2e/keyboard.spec.ts` (skip link, focus following navigation, every click-to-open row reachable by a link) — jsdom has no focus order, so none of it can live in Vitest, and a new click-to-navigate row or card gets a case there. A clean scan is a floor, not a verdict: axe judges only what is rendered, so overlays, the custom widgets the keyboard spec does not reach yet (the SQL editor, the lineage graph, drawer/modal focus return) and what a screen reader actually announces still need a browser check (the accessibility tree, not the DOM). Both lanes diff against the committed baseline `frontend/a11y-baseline.json` (shared logic in `frontend/scripts/a11y/ratchet.ts`) and fail ONLY on a violation not already in it — fixing what the baseline records is tracked separately, never silently re-added to the baseline to make a red run green. Regenerate the baseline deliberately, never by hand-editing the JSON, with `pnpm a11y:baseline` (needs the same CI-equivalent stack as `pnpm e2e` + `pnpm e2e:otp`; the otp phase needs no manual env — the script itself sets `E2E_OTP=1`) when a change to rendered markup is intentional — explain why in the PR.
56:5. **Definition of Done (DoD)** per task, in order:
70:6. **Trunk-based development** — branch off `main`, PR back to `main`. No long-lived `develop` or `release` branches.
71:7. **Branch naming:**
76:8. **`main` branch protection:** PR required + passing CI + no force-push. Approving-review count is 0 during solo-dev phase; re-enable (≥1) before onboarding a second contributor.
77:9. **Squash-merge only into `main`.** Keeps history linear and matches rule #1. Feature branch commit history is squashed into a single commit on merge.
78:10. **Conventional commits** for PR titles and the squash-merge commit message:
88:11. **PR template** checklist (`.github/pull_request_template.md`): manual test ✓, linked issue, security implications, schema migration. Its *Standards for new code* section is the checklist for rules 44–45.
89:12. **`CODEOWNERS`** (`.github/CODEOWNERS`) auto-routes reviews per area.
97:13. **Python:** Ruff (lint) → Black `--check` (format) → mypy (types) → Bandit (SAST) → pytest (from Week 8).
98:14. **Frontend:** ESLint → Prettier `--check` → Vitest (from Week 8).
99:15. **Secret scanning:** betterleaks in pre-commit hook AND in CI. A secret detected in CI blocks merge.
129:16. **SAST:** Bandit (Python) + CodeQL (GitHub Actions) on every PR. **Suppression hygiene (#806):** a suppression comment carries its test id and *nothing else* — put the justification on its own line above, and never spell `# nosec`/`# noqa` inside prose. Bandit parses everything after its token as a test-id list (so an inline explanation emits one warning per word, and merely *mentioning* the token in a nearby comment does the same); Ruff rejects the same shape as a malformed directive. **Judge a suppression by the gate's exit code, never by its warnings:** `bandit -c pyproject.toml -r backend/app/` (the CI command) must exit 0 with "No issues identified". A `nosec encountered … but no failed test` warning does **not** mean the suppression is dead — on a multi-line node bandit emits one per covered line that had no finding, so it is unavoidable noise around a load-bearing marker. Removing one on that evidence breaks the build; confirm against the exit code first.
130:17. **Dependency vulnerability scanning:** Dependabot alerts + auto-PRs for security updates, plus a synchronous CI gate (`pip-audit` backend, `pnpm audit` frontend). Python deps are pinned in `backend/requirements*.txt` (single source of truth; `environment.yml` and CI install from there).
138:18. **Python runtime:** `conda` only (`conda create -n dataq python=3.13`). Not venv, not poetry, not pyenv.
139:19. **Python formatter:** Black. Config in `pyproject.toml`. CI rejects unformatted code.
140:20. **Python linter:** Ruff. Replaces flake8 + isort + pyupgrade. Config in `pyproject.toml`.
141:21. **Python type checker:** mypy (strict mode). Config in `pyproject.toml`. When adding a new typed runtime import to `backend/app/`, pin the package in `backend/requirements.txt` and add the same pin to `backend/requirements-typecheck.txt` (the typed subset CI's mypy job installs). That is the whole list: the pre-commit ruff/black/mypy hooks are `language: system` and run the conda env's copies, so `.pre-commit-config.yaml` carries no versions of its own (#2080). `scripts/run-pinned-tool.py` refuses to run a hook whose env differs from those pins, and tells you to `conda env update`, so a local pass stays evidence of a CI pass.
142:22. **Frontend package manager:** pnpm. Not npm, not yarn.
143:23. **Frontend formatter:** Prettier. Config in `frontend/.prettierrc`.
144:24. **Frontend linter:** ESLint with TypeScript rules. Config in `frontend/eslint.config.cjs`.
145:25. **Config / 12-factor:** All environment-specific config via env vars. Backend uses Pydantic Settings (`backend/app/core/config.py`). Frontend uses Vite env vars (`VITE_*`). No env-specific code branches.
151:26. **Structured logging from Week 1.** `structlog` with JSON output. Every log entry carries a `request_id` correlation ID propagated FastAPI → Celery → GX. Configuration in `backend/app/core/logging.py`.
152:27. **PII redaction at the logger level** — not at every call site. Failed-check sample rows can contain sensitive data. The redactor in `backend/app/core/logging.py` strips known PII fields centrally.
153:28. **Consistent error shape** across all API responses. Definition in `backend/app/core/errors.py`:
157:29. **App Insights exception tracking wired from Week 1**, not Week 7. Middleware in `backend/app/main.py` captures all unhandled exceptions from the first commit; request/task spans and logs export through the vendor-neutral OpenTelemetry seam (`backend/app/core/tracing.py` + `core/otel.py` — App Insights on Azure, OTLP elsewhere).
163:30. **Backward-compatible migrations only.** No `DROP COLUMN` + code change in the same PR. Two-step deploys from Week 5 onward:
166:31. **Migration PR checklist:** rollback plan documented + "tested `alembic upgrade head` and `alembic downgrade -1` locally" ticked before requesting review.
168:32. **Read-modify-write is only as safe as its constraint.** There is no row-locking on the read-then-write paths today, so any "read current state → compute next → insert" sequence (e.g. the per-check `version_no` snapshot) can be raced by a concurrent writer. Guard each such write with a **unique constraint** (or `SELECT … FOR UPDATE`), and **catch the `IntegrityError`** to surface a **409** (reload + retry), not an unhandled 500 — e.g. `check_service.update_check` on `uq_check_versions_check_version`. `get_db` issues an explicit `rollback()` on any exception so a poisoned transaction never reaches the connection's next user.
174:33. **ADRs in `docs/site/adr/`** for every significant architecture decision. Use the `/adr-create` skill or follow the template in `docs/site/adr/README.md`. One short markdown per decision; keep it to 1–2 pages.
175:34. **Architecture diagram in `docs/site/architecture/overview.md`** (Mermaid). When a new component, datasource, or integration is added, update the diagram in the same PR as the code.
176:35. **Local setup script** `scripts/setup.sh` — one command from a fresh clone to a working dev environment (conda env + pre-commit install + docker-compose up + `alembic upgrade head` + seed data).
182:36. **End-of-week quick scan from Week 2 onward:** review Dependabot vuln alerts, secret scan results, OWASP top-10 spot check on any new endpoints, Key Vault access audit. The `/security-scan` skill (`.claude/skills/security-scan/`) runs this checklist.
183:37. **Hard security review gate before Week 7 deploy:** full pass on all of the above plus public-endpoint exposure review (especially `/api/v1/orchestration/events/*` and `/mcp`).
184:38. **Security vulnerabilities are not public GitHub issues.** Report via [GitHub Security Advisories](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/security/advisories/new). See [SECURITY.md](.github/SECURITY.md).
185:39. **Quarterly MCP supply-chain audit:** once a quarter, for each client-side MCP server pinned in `.mcp.json` (see CLAUDE.md Appendix), verify the package hasn't been deprecated, yanked, or transferred to a new publisher (e.g. `npm view <pkg> maintainers time`), and review the changelog before bumping the pinned major version. MCP servers run with local tool access — treat a publisher change like a compromised dependency until verified.
186:40. **Dependency license guardrail ([ADR 0031](docs/site/adr/0031-oss-byol-distribution-licensing.md)):** DataQ ships MIT — the dependency tree stays free of strong-copyleft and source-available licenses (GPL, AGPL, SSPL, BUSL/Elastic, Commons-Clause). Weak copyleft (LGPL/MPL/EPL) is acceptable with notice preservation. Adding a dependency that violates this needs an explicit ADR-level exception. Run the license sweep (backend: installed-env metadata; frontend: lockfile/`node_modules` license fields) alongside the rule-39 quarterly audit and before any release/image publish.
187:41. **Published docs (`docs/site/`, the `docs_dir` GitHub Pages build) never cite issue IDs or PR numbers** — no `#NNNN`, no `github.com/.../issues/…` or `/pull/…` links. Those are internal project-tracking artifacts with no meaning to an external reader of the public site; state the *behavior*, not the ticket that produced it. Also don't link a published page to an un-published internal doc (`README.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `docs/progress*.md`, `docs/retro*.md`, `docs/ops-log.md`) — those aren't reachable from the site and the link is dead weight for a reader outside the repo. Minimize cross-links from ordinary published pages into `docs/site/adr/` too: ADRs are design-rationale records for contributors, not the audience of a feature guide — link one only when the ADR itself is the answer to what the reader is asking, not as a routine "see also." **Within `docs/site/adr/`:** ADR-to-ADR references are fine (an ADR is allowed to cite another ADR it supersedes/amends/depends on — that's the decision graph, not project tracking). ADR-to-PR references should still be minimized — an ADR records *why a decision was made*, not *which PR shipped it*; a PR link ties a durable rationale to an ephemeral implementation artifact and is exactly the class rule 41 exists to keep out.
188:42. **Stable external surfaces follow the API compatibility policy** (`docs/site/reference/api-compatibility.md`): the REST API, MCP tools, the suite export document and the Python client (`dataq-client` and its CLI). An additive change needs nothing; a breaking change is announced under **Breaking** in the CHANGELOG, stays deprecated for at least one minor release before removal (security fixes excepted, still announced), and any suite-document shape change (an added field included) bumps its `version` while the previous version stays importable for a minor release. A PR that changes a stable surface says which kind of change it is.
189:43. **Changelog entries are fragments, assembled at release.** A PR never edits the Unreleased part of `docs/site/reference/changelog.md`; it adds `changelog.d/<issue>.<section>.md` (`<issue>-<n>` for a second entry; section one of `breaking | security | added | changed | fixed`; body = the bullet's text without the leading `- `, bold lead phrase, no ticket numbers — rule 41). The published page renders them under **Unreleased** at build time (`docs/hooks/changelog_fragments.py`). CI fails a PR that touches user-facing paths (`backend/app/`, `frontend/src/`, `packages/`, `integrations/`, `deploy/`, `docs/site/{guides,get-started,reference}/`) without a fragment unless it carries the **`no-changelog`** label; Dependabot is exempt. At release, `python scripts/changelog.py assemble --version X.Y.Z --date YYYY-MM-DD` moves the fragments into the dated section (the step is in the release checklist, `docs/site/operate/runbook-faq.md`). Grammar and examples: `changelog.d/README.md`.
190:44. **New code meets the standards already in force; a known gap is not a licence to widen it.** Open debt (the Week-7 accessibility audits #1672/#1673, any filed backlog item) is fixed on its own schedule, but a PR adds nothing to it. For UI, beyond rule 4b's automated floor: every new control is reachable and operable by keyboard, a dialog or drawer takes focus on open and returns it on close, every control and icon button has an accessible name, status that changes without navigation (a run, a save, an async result) is announced through a live region, a chart has a text or table alternative, colours come from the theme tokens in both themes, a new click-to-navigate row gets a `keyboard.spec.ts` case, and the change is checked in the browser's accessibility tree rather than the DOM. For the other surfaces, the existing bars apply to new code without exception: MCP tools state their blind spots (the `mcp-honesty-reviewer` agent on any change to `backend/app/mcp/server.py`), migrations follow rules 30–31 (the `migration-safety` agent), dependencies pass rule 40's licence gate, published docs follow rule 41, values crossing a driver boundary are tested in the shape the driver returns (the `driver-boundary-guard` agent), and secrets and PII follow rules 15, 15a and 27 and the review cadence in section H. Where a standard cannot be met in the PR, the PR says which and links the filed issue.
191:45. **Interfaces use the open standard that exists for them, and the check that enforces it stays green.** **OpenAPI:** every REST operation has a summary and a typed success response (`backend/tests/api/test_openapi_contract.py`), a file download declares its media types, and `docs/site/reference/openapi.json` plus the generated `dataq-client` are regenerated in the same PR (both drift checks run in CI). **OpenTelemetry:** traces, logs and metrics are emitted through the OTel SDK and exported over OTLP from `core/otel.py`; a vendor exporter lives only there, no proprietary APM SDK is added, attributes follow the OTel semantic conventions with DataQ's own under `dataq.*`, and usage events go through the closed vocabulary in `core/usage_telemetry.py` (`backend/tests/core/test_open_standard_seams.py` holds the import boundary). **OpenLineage:** lineage events are OpenLineage run events built in `backend/app/lineage/` (same test). **ODCS:** a data contract is read and written as an Open Data Contract Standard document (current major, v3); DataQ-specific fields go in its custom properties, never a parallel format. **OIDC** for sign-in, **SPDX** for the SBOM, the **Vault KV v2 API** for the secret store, **conventional commits** and the API compatibility policy (rule 42) for versioning. A new interface with no fitting standard records that in its ADR.

name: dataq-stacked-pr-after-squash-merge
description: "How to fix a stacked PR that goes CONFLICTING after its base PR squash-merges — merge main and resolve, never force-push"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: b8546e7c-0c8e-402c-b6cc-6720612adcfc
---

When PR B is branched off PR A's branch and **A squash-merges to `main`**, B's branch still carries A's *original* commits, which are not ancestors of main's squash commit. GitHub then reports B as `mergeable: CONFLICTING` / `DIRTY`, and its diff shows A's changes again.

**Do NOT fix this by rebasing + force-pushing.** The standing rule (see [[dataq-fixup-commits-in-review]]) forbids force-pushing an open PR, and the harness auto-mode classifier blocks both `git push --force-with-lease` on an open PR's branch and `git reset --hard` over a dirty tree.

**The fix that works and stays within the rules:**
```
git checkout -b tmp origin/<B-branch>     # branch at ORIGIN's B tip
git merge origin/main                      # conflicts = squash artifacts
# every conflict is "same content, two histories" — B's side is the superset
for f in $(git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U); do git checkout --ours -- "$f" && git add "$f"; done
git commit --no-edit
git diff origin/main...HEAD --stat         # VERIFY: only B's own files remain
git push origin tmp:<B-branch>             # normal push, no force → PR B updates
```
Always run that `git diff origin/main...HEAD --stat` check — it's what proves you took the superset and didn't silently drop anything main had.

**How to apply:** Prefer avoiding the situation — branch each PR off `main` when the files don't overlap. Stack only when they genuinely do, and expect this cleanup after the base merges.

Related: [[dataq-fixup-commits-in-review]], [[dataq-verify-locally-before-push]]

name: dev-always-branch-from-clean-main
description: "Always git checkout main + pull before creating a new fix/feature branch, even mid-chain — never branch off whatever you're currently sitting on"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: 69e80831-f1df-4b73-9124-56be4ce388ca
  modified: 2026-08-21T20:01:07.657Z

`git checkout -b <new-branch>` branches off whatever ref is currently checked out — not `main` — unless you explicitly switch first. Skipping that switch silently carries the current branch's commits into the new one.

**Why:** on 2026-08-21, working a chain of fix PRs (#1485 → #1486 → #1489), a docs-only PR (#1487) was opened and the user said "hold #1487, fix #1486 first." The next `git checkout -b fix/issue-1486-...` was run without first returning to `main` — still sitting on the #1487 docs branch — so #1487's held commit rode along into #1486's branch, and then squash-merged into `main` as part of #1486's PR (#1488), landing prematurely and out of the user's control. The contamination then propagated into the next branch in the chain (#1489) too, surfacing later as a spurious merge conflict against `main` (the classic squash-merge SHA-drift shape, [[dev-stacked-pr-after-squash-merge]], but caused by branch contamination rather than normal drift).

**How to apply:** before every `git checkout -b`, run `git checkout main && git pull --ff-only origin main` first — no exceptions, even "just one more quick branch" mid-chain. If a `git diff origin/main...HEAD --stat` on a new branch ever shows files you didn't intend to touch (especially a `docs/` file from an unrelated held PR), that's the tell — check `git log --oneline` on the new branch against `main` immediately rather than opening the PR. If contamination is later discovered already merged, the fix is: close the now-redundant original PR (don't try to merge it — it'd be a no-op or conflict), and note the process gap in the next progress-snapshot update rather than silently absorbing it.

Related: a CONFLICTING PR gets ZERO GitHub Actions runs at all (no test-merge commit → no `pull_request` events) — presents as "CI stopped scheduling", not as an error. Fix is the same either way: merge `origin/main` into the branch, resolve, push — CI resumes immediately. See `project_w6_close_state.md`'s "CONFLICTING-PR-kills-CI gotcha" note.

2026-09-05: bit again on #1900 — three pushes, zero CI runs, close/reopen did nothing; the PR had gone CONFLICTING against main (changelog). Check `gh pr view N --json mergeable` FIRST when CI is silent.
